A prototype-based metric-learning model for sea-ice type mapping from Sentinel-1 SAR and ancillary data
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Limited labeled data remains a central challenge for deep-learning-based sea-ice type mapping, while cross-channel relationships remain underexploited, and interaction mechanisms are lacking. This study proposes ESICM, combining Sentinel-1 SAR, AMSR2 brightness temperatures, and ERA5 environmental variables for pixel-level mapping of open water (OW), young ice (YI), first-year ice (FYI), and multi-year ice (MYI). ESICM adopts prototype-based metric learning to fully exploit labels, incorporates a channel multiplication-division module to enhance cross-channel interactions, and introduces two interaction functions, supports-input selection and user dense prompts, to improve classification in hard-to-classify scenes. On the AI4Arctic dataset, trained on 492 AI4Arctic scenes and tested on 20 scenes, ESICM achieved 93.34% overall accuracy, 93.08% F1 score (F1), 88.40% Kappa coefficient, and 77.29% mean intersection over union, exceeding the second-best results by 0.85%–1.55%. Under challenging melt-affected conditions, MYI F1 and intersection over union exceeded the second-best results by 3.13% and 3.93%. Across forward-temporal, cross-region, reduced-training-data, and cross-dataset experiments, ESICM ranked first for 14 and second for two of 16 metrics, indicating relatively strong generalization. In two hard-to-classify scenes, simulated user prompts covering 10% of valid pixels improved all four metrics by more than 4% and 20% over prompt-free inference, respectively, supporting the technical feasibility of interaction. SHAP attributions were broadly consistent with established sea-ice remote-sensing knowledge, enhancing the model’s post hoc interpretability. Overall, ESICM improved sea-ice mapping with limited labeled data and showed application potential under controlled distribution shifts and simulated interaction.

title: Enhancing soil property retrieval in an Ali-Perudic Argosols–dominated region through multi-angle hyperspectral feature integration
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Soil bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) is strongly influenced by soil physicochemical properties, yet most hyperspectral retrieval studies rely on single-view reflectance, leaving the value of multi-angle information insufficiently explored. In this study, bidirectional reflectance factors (BRFs) were measured at 48 viewing angles for 156 soil samples collected from a region dominated by Ali-Perudic Argosols. An optimal multi-angle retrieval framework was developed for different soil properties by systematically comparing spectral preprocessing methods, feature extraction, and modeling algorithms. The effects of viewing angle on retrieval accuracy and feature wavelength distribution were further analyzed, and the applicability of simulated multi-angle BRFs generated using SOILSPECT model was further assessed. Results show that the optimal framework for single-view reflectance combines Savitzky–Golay (SG) smoothing, a hybrid random frog–competitive adaptive reweighted sampling (RFROG–CARS) feature selection strategy, and nonlinear support vector machine (SVM) regression. Retrieval accuracy varied substantially with viewing geometry, and no universal optimal viewing angle was identified across soil properties. For multi-angle BRF data, a two-dimensional convolutional neural network (2D-CNN) feature extraction approach outperformed the RFROG–CARS wavelength selection method. Specifically, R 2 (RMSE) improved from 0.64 (8.8 g/kg) to 0.73 (7.7 g/kg) for SOM content, from 0.53 (6.9 %) to 0.61 (6.3 %) for sand content, and from 0.64 (4.7 %) to 0.69 (4.4 %) for silt content, while remaining comparable for cation exchange capacity (0.77/2.4 cmol/kg to 0.76/2.4 cmol/kg) and clay content (0.80/4.3 % to 0.79/4.3 %). Although the retrieval accuracy based on multi-angle BRFs remained slightly lower than that obtained from the optimal viewing geometry, it consistently outperformed most individual viewing angles. The selected multi-angle hyperspectral features were distributed across nearly all viewing angles, indicating complementary spectral–geometric information. Although retrieval accuracy based on simulated BRFs was lower than that based on measured BRFs, the results were broadly comparable. These findings support the use of multi-angle information in soil spectroscopy and remote sensing applications.
